opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing that struck me was how *normal* they felt, in a good way. If you've spent time in AI labs in San Francisco, you walk into these offices in Beijing or Hangzhou and the vibe is surprisingly familiar. Open floor plans, lots of young researchers, monitors everywhere showing training curves and eval dashboards, people grabbing snacks and talking about papers. The research culture felt very legible to me.

That said, a few things stood out. The teams felt *young*. A lot of the people doing the core work were fresh out of PhD programs or even still students, and they had a lot of ownership over big pieces of the model pipeline. That's similar to the best labs in the US, but it was striking how consistent it was.

There was also a real sense of efficiency and focus. Less of the polished, venture-funded aesthetic you sometimes see in the Bay Area, fewer flashy amenities, and more "this is where we work, and we're here to ship models." The conversations reflected that too. People wanted to talk details: data mixtures, RL infrastructure, post-training recipes, how they think about evaluation. Very technical, very open about the craft, even if obviously not about everything.

And the thing I keep coming back to is how closely they follow what's happening in the West. They read every paper, they know the open-model ecosystem inside and out, and many have been influenced by things like the open post-training work we've done. So it didn't feel like visiting some separate universe. It felt like visiting another branch of the same research community, just under different constraints, particularly around compute, and those constraints have pushed them to be really clever about efficiency.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the Chinese labs with Bay Area offices, describing fewer flashy amenities and a less polished, venture-funded aesthetic. This communicates a difference in showroom-like office culture.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing that struck me was how normal they felt. I think a lot of people in the US have this picture of Chinese AI labs as either these secretive, state-run facilities or these scrappy operations running on borrowed hardware, and neither of those matched what I saw. You walk into a place like DeepSeek or Qwen's team at Alibaba or Moonshot, and it looks like a tech office. Open floor plans, whiteboards covered in architecture diagrams, people in hoodies arguing about data mixes. If you dropped me in there blindfolded, I'm not sure I could tell you whether I was in Beijing or San Francisco.

What was different was the energy and the density. The teams are young, maybe younger on average than what you see at the frontier labs here, and a lot of them came straight out of the top Chinese universities into these roles. There's a real sense that they're building something and that the window is open right now. Some of that is the DeepSeek effect. Once that moment happened, everyone in the ecosystem felt like the world was paying attention, and that shows up in how people carry themselves.

The other thing I'd flag is how serious they are about open models, and not as a marketing position. When you talk to researchers there, open weights are just the default assumption about how you ship. That's a cultural difference from a lot of the US labs, where open releases are the exception you have to justify. In China it's closer to the other way around.

And then there's the hardware reality, which you can feel in conversations even if you don't see it in the office. People are very thoughtful about compute efficiency because they have to be. The constraints are real, and they talk about them openly. It's shaped the research culture in ways that I think the rest of the world is only starting to appreciate.

r001.rationale: The response describes the offices as normal tech workplaces and names other differences, but it does not identify showroom culture as a difference.
